title: Interpreting Image-based Profiles using Similarity Clustering and Single-Cell Visualization
protocol: Perform feature selection to exclude features with low variance (frequency cut = 0.05).
Exclude features highly correlated with another feature in the profile (threshold = 0.9).
Remove features with more than 5% NA values.
Eliminate blocklisted features from the dataset.
Identify and remove outliers (features with minimum or maximum absolute values greater than threshold = 500).
Clone the GitHub repository into your computer or download the repository from the provided URL.
Access the Morpheus website at https://software.broadinstitute.org/morpheus/.
Click on "Select File" and select the Morpheus_Example_FeatureSelected.gct file downloaded from GitHub.
On the main screen, click on Options (gear symbol) > Annotations tab > Column annotations.
Deselect id and select Compound, Concentration, MOA, Wells, and Plate.
Right-click on the column labels (Compound, Concentration, MOA, Wells, and Plate) and enable “Show color” for all the columns.
Avoid these steps by using the Morpheus_Example_FeatureSelected.json file instead.
Click on Options > Color Scheme.
De-select the Relative color scheme.
Change the minimum to –1000 and the maximum to 1000.
Try also with –100 and 100.
Close the Option window.
Click the zoom tool.
Select Fit To Window.
Use the mouse pointer to scroll through the row names in the right corner of the screen, highlighting feature names.
Remove unusual features colored red or blue carefully as they may indicate errors during image acquisition.
Select Options > Color Scheme and choose Relative color scheme to use minimum and maximum values in each row for coloring.
Calculate the correlation between wells for all pairs of features using Tools > Similarity Matrix > Pearson correlation on the rows.
Click on Options > Display and select Link rows and columns.
Create a Hierarchical Clustering by selecting Tools > Hierarchical Clustering.
In Metric, select “Matrix values (for a pre-computed similarity matrix)”.
Change Cluster to Rows and Columns.
Click OK to group the features based on their profile similarities using the chosen correlation metric.
Scroll down to look for red squares along the diagonal that denote high correlation.
Check the names of features in those rows and columns.
Type "id: Nuclei_AreaShape_Extent" next to the Help menu in the white box and hit Enter.
Click on the arrows next to "Nuclei_AreaShape_Extent" to redirect to the feature and see it highlighted.
Go back to the first tab “Morpheus_Example_FeatureSelected”.
Select Tools > Similarity Matrix > Pearson correlation on the columns.
Click on Options > Display and select Link rows and columns.
While holding the shift key, click on the MOA, Compound, and Concentration columns (in this order).
Sort them by value.
Go to the microtubule inhibitor and microtubule-stabilizing agent MOAs (Fig. 2A).
See how there are large squares colored in red when comparing the correlation coefficient for both groups, meaning these two MOAs are closely correlated and produce similar morphological profiles.
Distinguish subtle effects of drug concentration: the lowest concentration of microtubule stabilizer is relatively dissimilar from all concentrations of microtubule inhibitor.

Note that at higher microtubule stabilizer doses, the phenotype is indistinguishable from low concentrations of microtubule inhibitor but less similar to higher concentrations of microtubule inhibitor.
Look for more unusual correlations.
Sort the collapsed similarity matrix by MOA and by plate by holding the shift key.
Zoom out (pressing the minus – key) to see a broader view of the matrix.
Roll over to the DMSO MOA (the negative control in this dataset).
Observe the distribution of DMSO samples.
Note that DMSO samples do not have universally high correlations with each other.
Notice that some DMSO samples are correlated by well position.
Recognize that plate normalization was performed using DMSO as the baseline.
Understand that DMSO is not a phenotype in this dataset and all DMSO profiles should have feature values of zero, apart from technical noise.
Identify correlations between DMSO samples related to their positions within plates.
Create a hierarchical clustering by selecting Tools > Hierarchical Clustering.
Select “Matrix values (from a pre-computed similarity matrix)” in Metric.
Change Cluster to Rows and Columns.
Click OK to group samples based on their profile similarity.
Zoom out using the – key to see a broader view of the clustering.
Scroll through the matrix to find large squares of red color.
Observe which MOAs are clustering.
Sort the p value column by right-clicking on it.
Explore the names of the features that determine the difference between DMSO and tubulin polymerization inhibitors.
If you have a large number of features with a p value of 0.00, these will continue to be sorted alphabetically and not by strength.
In this case, sort to find the highest and lowest T-test values, which should represent the strongest features.
Go back to the similarity matrix.
Go to File > Save Dataset.
Write a name for your file.
Click OK to save as GCT version 1.3.
Save the table to allow it to be opened again in Morpheus when needed.
Use a script to retrieve random or representative images from the dataset.
Plot retrieved images together for observation.
Choose which samples to observe based on their characteristics.
Group and display chosen samples according to user preference.
Perform clustering analysis on the morphological space of single cells.
Sample from subpopulations closest to the center of the sample(s) of interest.
Compute similarity matrices using Jupyter Notebook.
Examine experiments using per-well aggregated information for large-scale studies.
Open the Google Colab notebook Basic Protocol 2 from the GitHub repository.
Click the Copy to Drive button to make a copy available in your Google Drive.
Run the first three cells in the notebook Section 1 - Import Libraries.
Click on the start button at the top left or hit Ctrl + Enter.
Clone the GitHub repository and install the functions.
Install required libraries to run this notebook and import them.
Run only the first cell inside Section 2 - Define Inputs.
Define inputs required to run the cells in the notebook.
Provide filename and pathname to access the CSV table and read it as a DataFrame.
Provide pathname for the images directory.
Import the dataset inside Section 3a.
Perform annotation of the dataset.
Normalize the dataset.
Select features from the dataset.
Map measurement data to treatment metadata.
Load the annotated and normalized dataset directly in Section 3B if already processed.
Run normalization on the whole dataset or relative to the negative control.
Run the first three cells in Section 4 through cell 4.1.1.
Choose Metadata_Compound_Concentration for this demonstration.
Add the “Metadata_” prefix to any columns before loading new data into the notebook.
Use dropdown interaction to allow different choices based on DataFrame content.
Run the cell in Section 4.2 to choose all compounds available on the dataset for visualization.
Select only a few compounds of interest by running Section 4.3 and choosing from interactive checkboxes.
Generate and graph the correlation between compounds using cells in Section 5.
Choose a column to be the labels for the correlation matrix using the dropdown menu.
Use pycytominer to return a per-well aggregated DataFrame.
Export the generated correlation matrix as an image by typing its name.
Run the first cell to choose whether to visualize randomly selected or representative single cells.
Choose the random method to select random samples for each treatment/group.
Choose the representative method to select the most representative cell within each subgroup.
Rerun those cells before returning to Section 6 and running all cells here if changing reference compounds.
Use the KMeans algorithm with the scikit-learn package to cluster data and find the most representative cell(s).
The random method will return a random sample of one cell for each subgroup.
Run the next cell and select how many cells you would like to display from each subgroup.
Choose whether or not you would like the images shown in order of subgroup correlation to the reference compound.

Answering “Yes” to “Would you like to use the correlations to order your image plot?” will order the dataset based on the correlation values to the reference compound selected, starting at 1.0 and descending.
Answering “No” will keep the DataFrame in the original order.
Choose how many cells (c) to plot for each group.
Choose whether each image should be rescaled to the minimum and maximum before being displayed.
Choose whether the raw intensity values should be plotted.
Insert the pixel size value in μm/pixel for adding a scale bar in images.
Type "0.29898" as the pixel size value for this example dataset.
Plot the selected single cells in random order by running the first cell of Section 6.1.
Explore the images before knowing to which group the cells belong.
Run the rest of the cells in Section 6.1 to append labels and check hypotheses.
Create an unshuffled version of the image.
Save the image to disk.
Examine cells without labels to formulate new hypotheses.
Analyze organelle distribution within the cells.
Observe organization of mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, and Golgi apparatus.
Evaluate changes in overall intensity of individual stains.
Assess changes in overall cell structure.
Run Section 6.2 to display full images from which single-cell crops have been pulled.
Examine entire field of view (FOV) for additional biological insights.
Look at whole images to assess the overall cell shape and size distributions.
Determine how cells were affected by treatment.
Compare cell sizes relative to negative control.
Analyze changes in cell shape.
Evaluate whether cells appear more elongated or rounder.
Assess cell density within FOV.
Determine if perturbations induce proliferative signaling pathways.
Identify if perturbations reduce cell viability.
